                    ### Question
                    A 32-year-old woman comes to her doctor’s office with abdominal distention, diffuse abdominal pain, and a history of 10–12 bowel movements a day for the last week. She was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease 3 years ago. Today, vitals are normal. Her abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender to palpation. A CT scan shows evidence of a fistula and strictures located in the last 30 cm of her ileum. A resection of the affected portion of the bowel is scheduled. What changes in bile metabolism are expected in this patient post-procedure?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Absorption of vitamin K will not be impaired
opb. Synthesis of cholesterol in the liver will decrease
opc. The balance of the components in bile will be altered
opd. Enteric bacteria will remain the same in the small intestine
ope. Absorption of  7⍺-dehydroxylated bile will decrease

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Following the resection of the ileum in a patient with Crohn's disease, significant changes in bile metabolism are expected due to the removal of the primary site for bile acid absorption. This leads to decreased reabsorption of bile acids, resulting in an increased loss of bile acids in feces and a compensatory increase in bile acid synthesis by the liver. Consequently, the balance of the components in bile will be altered (opc). Additionally, the reduced absorption of bile acids means less substrate is available for bacterial conversion in the intestine, leading to decreased absorption of 7⍺-dehydroxylated bile acids (ope). The evidence paths regarding the role of the ileum in vitamin K absorption and its impact on intestinal bacteria, while correct, do not directly support or refute the specific changes in bile metabolism post-resection. Therefore, these paths do not alter the conclusions drawn from the medical consensus on the effects of ileum resection on bile metabolism.
